title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of what many consider Charles Dickens's most intricate, most modern, and most unsettling novel.

Our Mutual Friend was Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1864 and 1865, and it gave the world the Thames as a highway of death, the dust heap as a monument to inherited wealth, and some of the most psychologically vivid characters he ever drew.
Over the course of this series, three remarkable readers will help us unpack it — its craft, its characters, its moral imagination, and its extraordinary strangeness.
First, Dr. Eleanor Hartley — a novelist and creative writing teacher who brings a practitioner's eye to Dickens's architecture.
When Eleanor reads a sentence, she's asking: how did he do that?
Sir Edmund Leigh joins us — a retired Oxford don whose convictions about the moral imagination in fiction are both deeply held and beautifully argued.
Edmund reads Dickens as a novelist of human character under pressure — not as a social reformer with a pen.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and lifelong devotee of this novel, who has re-read it more times than she will admit.
Caroline is our guide to what it feels like to actually read these pages — what stops you, what moves you, what makes you read a sentence twice.
Today we begin at the beginning — or rather, at the foundations: the dust heaps, the river, the atmosphere of wealth, death, and obsession that Dickens builds from page one.
What strikes me, coming back to this novel, is how immediately Dickens establishes his central irony — that money and rubbish are, in his world, the same substance.
The dust heaps are the source of the Boffin fortune, and Dickens never lets you forget it.
Look at how he introduces Nicodemus Boffin — the language is doing so much work at once.
"The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour, or in less cutting language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, the Golden Dustman."
That parenthetical — "or in less cutting language" — is Dickens winking at his own narrator.
He's saying: I know exactly how savage this description is, and I'm choosing it deliberately.
The narration already has a double consciousness — satirical and fond at the same time.
I take your point about the narration, Eleanor, though I'd enter a small caveat.
The fondness you identify is not merely authorial strategy — it reflects something genuine about Boffin's moral situation.
Here is a man of essentially good nature who has been thrust, without preparation, into a position of grotesque excess.
The image Dickens reaches for is perfectly chosen.
"Like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites."
The aristocracy reduced to an overripe cheese — and the parasites who live off it.
It is devastating, and it is also, I think, entirely just.
Boffin is the novel's moral centre — not because he is clever, but because he is genuinely kind.
What I love about that cheese image is that it's funny — properly funny — and then the joke keeps unspooling into something darker.
Boffin calls the parasites a sort of "perpetual Legacy Duty" — he's resigned to it, even cheerful about it.
But later in the novel we see what that same money does to less good-natured souls entirely.
There's a passage with Silas Wegg that I think is the dark twin of this Boffin scene.
"Power — unless it be the power of intellect or virtue — has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures."
Same house, same money — but look at what it becomes in Wegg's hands.
Boffin's resigned good humour and Wegg's gleeful malice — they're two poles of the novel's moral universe.
That juxtaposition is so precise — and I think Dickens earns it structurally.
Wegg is positioned as the Evil Genius over Boffin's house — those are the narrator's own words — and the comedy of his villainy is inseparable from his pettiness.
He has to hover over the house at night just to feel powerful.
The power fantasy is completely hollow — and Dickens shows us its hollowness through the very grandiosity of the narrator's description.
It's one of those moments where the style IS the argument.
Wegg is a fascinating study in the corrupting effect of a single, mean desire.
He is not a grand villain — which is precisely the point.
Dickens understands that moral failure is usually small and squalid, not large and dramatic.
The novel also gives us a very different register of darkness — in the extraordinary figure of John Harmon.
A man who reads his own death notice.
That is not satire — that is something altogether more vertiginous.
The Harmon passages are where I think the novel becomes something genuinely frightening.
He finds a placard at Whitehall announcing his own death — his own body, described, lying in a mortuary.
And then — in the most chilling sentence — he pieces together what must have happened.

"I perceived that Radfoot had been murdered by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me, and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark place into the same dark tide."
"The same dark place into the same dark tide" — that repetition is devastating.
It collapses two men — murderer and intended victim — into a single terrible symmetry.
The river doesn't distinguish between them.
And the river as indifferent moral force runs through the whole novel — it's there in the very opening pages, with the corpse-scavengers on the Thames.
But there's another register of gothic dread in the novel that I think is even more psychologically acute — Bradley Headstone.
The passage where his face creeps up the staircase in the dark — outside Wrayburn's chambers — is extraordinary.
"The haggard head floated up the dark staircase, and softly descended nearer to the floor outside the outer door of the chambers."
That verb — floated — detaches the head from the body.
Bradley is so consumed by obsession that he has become almost spectral — the grammar of the sentence does that before you've consciously noticed.
That passage ends with a line that haunts me every time I read it.

"If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of the night."
Dickens gives us what the character cannot see — and that gap between knowledge and ignorance is where all the danger lives.
Lightwood is sleeping peacefully a few feet from something monstrous.
It's one of those passages that makes you realise Dickens could have written horror fiction, and the world would have been a more frightened place.
So in just a handful of passages, we already have the full emotional range of this novel — comic, satirical, gothic, tragic.
Money and dust and the Thames — connected, as Edmund says, by an indifferent force that treats murderer and victim alike.
We'll be exploring all of that in the segments ahead.
After the break, we turn to the novel's great love stories — and the question of whether Dickens's romantic imagination was equal to his satirical one.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're diving into one of Dickens's most psychologically rich portraits: Bella Wilfer and her troubled relationship with money.
Bella begins the novel as a self-declared mercenary — frank about her hunger for wealth, almost defiant about it.
And yet something keeps interrupting that hunger — a moral instinct she can't quite silence.
With me to unpick all of this are three wonderful readers of this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley brings her novelist's eye for the architecture of how Dickens builds this transformation sentence by sentence.
Sir Edmund Leigh reads Bella as a story about individual character tested by temptation — moral imagination at full stretch.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who has lived with this novel since her teens, attends above all to the emotional truth — what it feels like to be Bella in these scenes.
Eleanor, let's start with you — because the passage where Mr Boffin advises Bella to 'go in for money' is extraordinary.
What is Dickens doing there, structurally and tonally?
What strikes me immediately is how Dickens gives Mr Boffin that repeated, almost incantatory rhythm.
Listen to the cadence of it — he sets up the quote like a conjuror presenting the trick:
'Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.'
The word 'money' appears four times in three sentences.
That's not accident — that's Dickens hammering a nail into the reader's skull, making the repetition itself feel like corruption.
And then that extraordinary final syllable — Boffin doesn't just say 'rich,' he rolls it: 'R—r—rich!'
Dickens renders the very sound of greed on the page — something almost physical, like an animal savoring meat.
Eleanor is quite right about the phonology — and I'd add that what makes the scene morally interesting is Bella's position as audience to it.
Because Dickens has already prepared us, in the preceding passage, for what this speech costs Boffin — or rather, what it reveals he has become.
The narrator shows us Bella stealing a glance at him — and what she sees is described with that wonderful precision:
'a dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.'
The phrase 'once open face' is the moral sting.
Dickens is insisting that this is a fall — that something genuinely good in Boffin has been eclipsed.
And Bella witnesses it — which sets the question the whole arc must answer: will she follow him down, or resist?
What I keep returning to is what happens when Bella is alone in her room after all of this.
Because Dickens gives her a scene of genuine self-interrogation — and it's both funny and quietly devastating.
She goes to the looking-glass — her habitual tribunal — and she puts herself on trial.

'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
The comedy is real — she calls herself a 'Beast' with complete seriousness.
But the moral discomfort underneath is equally real.
She can't quite own the values she thought were hers — and that gap is where her transformation begins.
Caroline, that scene is one of the great Dickensian set-pieces for a character catching herself in bad faith.
And what's technically remarkable is that Dickens uses free indirect discourse — we're inside Bella's mind, not merely observing her.
The word 'somehow' opens the scene twice — 'Somehow, Bella was not so well pleased' — and that 'somehow' is doing enormous work.
It signals that Bella herself doesn't understand her own reaction — she's ahead of her own self-knowledge.
That's psychologically very sophisticated — more so than Dickens is usually credited for.
I think we should resist the temptation to overload this with theoretical apparatus.
What Dickens is depicting is something moralists have always understood: the conscience operating against the will's declared intentions.
Johnson said that almost all absurdity of conduct arises from the imitation of those whom we cannot resemble.
Bella wants to resemble the rich and fashionable — but her character is better than that ambition.
The 'inconsistent little Beast' is not a psychological paradox — she is simply a good young woman who has temporarily misdirected herself.
I want to bring Lizzie Hexam into this, because I think she's the catalyst Bella needs — and the contrast between them is heartbreaking.
When Bella hears Lizzie speak about Eugene, with that complete selflessness — the love that asks for nothing in return — she turns on herself.
And Dickens gives us that wonderful moment of comic self-flagellation — she actually pokes herself in the side.
But before that, she has heard Lizzie say something extraordinary:
'I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.'
Lizzie is talking about a love she expects will never be returned — and she calls it light.
Beside that, Bella's whole worldview — beauty, money, the Boffin programme — suddenly looks very thin.
And the penitential poke in the side is brilliant because it's ridiculous and sincere at once.
Dickens quotes her own internal rebuke verbatim:
'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?'
The colloquial 'Ain't' is so perfectly chosen — it's Bella puncturing her own social pretensions in the very act of moral recovery.
She slips into a more honest, less polished idiom when she's genuinely feeling something.
That's a very fine touch.
I want to draw attention to a passage that stands behind all of this — one that establishes what the life of greed and drink actually produces in a human being.
Lizzie's description of the child in her care — surrounded by drunkards from birth — is not incidental local colour.
It is the novel's moral baseline — the terminal destination of a life lived without virtue or care for others.
Lizzie tells her brother:
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthesis — 'if she ever had one' — is devastating.
It suggests the child may never have known even the most rudimentary tenderness.
Against that — against that — Bella's complaints about not being rich enough seem rather less sympathetic.
Edmund, that's exactly right — and I think Dickens intends that contrast to be felt, not merely noted.
Bella has never gone hungry, never wanted a cradle — and yet she has constructed a grievance around wealth as profound as anyone's.
What saves her — what the novel insists can save any of us — is the capacity to feel shame when confronted by someone whose goodness is larger than your own.
Lizzie is that person for Bella — and Bella is humble enough to recognise it.
What a thread this has been — from Boffin's unctuous 'R—r—rich' to that child who may never have had a cradle.
Bella's arc sits at the centre of this novel's argument about what money does to character — and what character can do to resist money.
Coming up, we'll follow that thread further — into the world of the Veneerings and the social performance of wealth.
Stay with us.

segments.title: A Dead Man's Fortune: Plot, Secrecy, and Identity

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We're deep in the labyrinth of identity and inheritance that sits at the heart of this novel.
Today's segment is about the secret at the centre of everything: a dead man's fortune, a living man's disguise, and the question of who actually deserves what Old Harmon left behind.
With me are three readers who know this novel intimately.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who never stops noticing how Dickens builds his effects — the architecture of a sentence, the weight of a single image.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Dickens as a moralist first and foremost — always asking what the novel reveals about individual character under pressure.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and brings the reader's eye — alert to what moves you, what makes you laugh, what demands to be read aloud.
Let's begin where so much of the novel's emotional power begins — with the Boffins, and what they witnessed of young John Harmon's childhood.
What strikes me every time I return to Boffin's account of young John Harmon is the sheer physical tenderness of it.
Dickens gives us a seven-year-old child, alone, going off to a foreign school, coming into the Boffins' yard just to warm himself by their fire.
And the detail of his little scanty travelling clothes — that word, scanty, used twice in two sentences — it breaks your heart.
Boffin sets it up like this — and I want to read it at length, because the rhythm matters.
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat."
That anaphora — There was, there was — it's a lament.
Boffin isn't a literary man, but grief has given him the cadences of an elegy.
Caroline is right to dwell on the music of it, but I think we should be equally attentive to what Dickens is doing morally in that passage.
Mrs Boffin's spontaneous gesture — warming her hands, rubbing the child's cheeks — is an act of pure disinterested love.
She has no claim on this boy, no duty in the strict sense.
And yet she says something quite extraordinary.
"I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"
That repetition — wide wide world — is not literary affectation. It is the speech of someone overwhelmed.
What Dickens is arguing here, quietly but with great conviction, is that moral worth is not a function of station.
The Boffins earn their fortune, in the truest sense, long before any will is proved.
Edmund's point about earned moral worth makes me want to look at the earlier passage — the one about Old Harmon's cruelty — because Dickens is doing something structurally brilliant there.
He wants to establish the Boffins as protectors, not beneficiaries, before we get anywhere near the question of the will.
And he does it through pure comedy of detail — which then tips, without warning, into something genuinely shocking.
Listen to how Boffin describes Old Harmon's rage.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard."
The parenthetical about the bonnet is pure Dickensian comedy — the comic detail buffering the violence — and then it's gone.
"Received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
Three sentences. Three blows. The repetition of 'Dropped her' is both rhythmic and brutal — Boffin barely able to say it once, so he says it again.
That moment sits very close to comedy and very close to violence at the same time — which is so characteristic of how Dickens manages Old Harmon.
But of course the Boffins' inheritance is only one half of the plot's secret machinery.
The other half is the question of who John Harmon actually is — and Dickens, unusually, steps forward in his own voice to address this directly.
The authorial postscript — what Dickens calls his note about the story's design — is one of the most fascinating moments of craft transparency in Victorian fiction.
He's responding, in advance, to readers who accused him of withholding information he was actually signalling.
And he puts his case with wonderful exactness.

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
The chiasmus — conceal what he was suggesting, suggest what readers thought he was concealing — is doing real argumentative work.
He's saying: the mystery was always in plain sight, if you trusted the artist.
I find the tone of that note rather more poignant than defiant.
Dickens is acutely aware that serialised reading creates a different kind of attention — impatient, suspicious, hunting for plot rather than resting in meaning.
He asks his readers, with admirable dignity, to extend to the artist a little patience.
That phrase — concede him a little patience — is almost Burkean in its appeal to trust and continuity.
Great art, like good government, cannot always explain its workings in the moment.
What I love is that the disguise — John Rokesmith living in the Boffins' house as their secretary — is so emotionally legible once you know it.
He is not concealing himself from them. He is, in some sense, returning to the only people who ever loved him.
That child who rested his heart against Mrs Boffin's bosom — he comes back, as a grown man, and takes his place in their household.
And Dickens gives us one of those extraordinary lines — the child looking up, quote, 'as if it was in pain — in agony.'
That look never leaves him, and it never leaves the Boffins.
And yet the novel doesn't let sentiment be the last word on John Harmon's story.
There is a reckoning coming — and it involves a Dutch bottle, a scoundrel called Wegg, and a revelation about property that changes everything.
The confrontation between Harmon and Wegg in the final chapters is one of those set-pieces where Dickens lets the plot's moral logic snap completely shut.
Wegg thinks he has leverage — a will hidden in a dust heap that he believes supersedes the one Boffin has proved.
And Harmon demolishes him with a sentence of magnificent compression.

"It is a will of my late father's, of more recent date than the will proved by Mr Boffin (address whom again, as you have addressed him already, and I'll knock you down), leaving the whole of his property to the Crown."
The parenthetical threat — knock you down — dropped right into the middle of legal language — is vintage Dickens.
The formality and the fury, held together in a single sentence.
What I find almost joyful in these scenes is the controlled physical violence.
Harmon is knocking Wegg's head against the wall — literally — and lecturing him at the same time.
He says, and this is wonderful —
"I mean to knock your head against the wall, and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out."
The comedy of the sum — a thousand pounds, precise, offhand — makes the menace funnier, and therefore more frightening.
Justice, in Dickens, is rarely abstract. It tends to come with a thud.
I don't dissent from the comedy, but I want to note what Dickens is doing beneath it.
Harmon tells Wegg precisely how he was watched — and the revelation is itself a form of punishment, carefully designed.
He explains, with a kind of prosecutorial relish —
"I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow."
Sloppy — the foundling, the child of charity — has been Harmon's instrument of surveillance all along.
There is a moral geometry here that Dickens has been constructing very patiently.
The dispossessed watch over the dispossessor. The weak confound the cunning.
That moral geometry, as Edmund calls it, is what makes the plot feel earned rather than merely ingenious.
John Harmon's secret isn't just a mystery to be solved. It's a test — of who deserves what the dust heaps have produced.
In our next segment, we'll look at how money and refuse intertwine in Dickens's vision of Victorian society — and what the dust heaps themselves mean.

segments.title: The Comedy of Manners: Dickens's Satirical Eye

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time with the novel's darker currents — the river, the dust, the dead.
Now we turn to something that makes this book genuinely, riotously funny.
Dickens's satirical eye — the comedy of manners, of hypocrisy, of greed performing itself on a very small stage.
Caroline Woodcourt has been our guide to the experience of reading this novel — the moments that make you laugh, that make you stop and re-read.
And on a subject like this, she's our natural anchor.
Caroline, where do you want to begin?
I want to begin with the Lammles, because they're one of Dickens's most perfectly constructed comic traps.
Two people who have each married the other for money they don't have — locked into a performance of affection that they both know is fraudulent.
And Dickens, being Dickens, gives us the satirical image that captures everything.
"How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them!"
And then — the killer turn — he writes:
"Now, if the skeleton up-stairs had taken that opportunity, for instance, of calling out 'Here I am, suffocating in the closet!'"
The skeleton in the closet — the fraud, the sham marriage — made literal, made to speak.
It's a joke and a chill at the same time.
What I love about that passage is the timing — the exclamation mark after 'How delightful,' which is pure performance itself.
Dickens is mimicking the Lammles' own theatrical excess in the very syntax of the narration.
And then the parenthetical — 'for instance' — that little cushion of mock-reasonableness makes it devastating.
The narrator pretends to be merely floating a hypothetical while actually stabbing them clean through.
One observes that Dickens is also doing something morally exact there, not merely witty.
The Lammles are not simply frauds — they have chosen to sustain the fraud, to perform it together, in a kind of mutual complicity.
The skeleton is not merely a metaphor for their finances — it is their shared moral condition.
And Dickens is precise about this: the image is comic, but the judgment is not.
That tension — comedy as a vehicle for moral judgment — runs all through the novel's gallery of comic villains.
And Silas Wegg is perhaps the most elaborately comic of them all.
Caroline, you've been looking closely at Wegg's great scheme — his plan to extort Boffin.
Wegg's plan is one of the great set-pieces of comic villainy in English fiction.
He addresses his partner Mr Venus as 'comrade, brother, and partner' — three times, relentlessly — with such solemn grandeur.
And the genius of it is in what he calls Boffin: 'the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour.'
But the real masterpiece is the price he announces.
"He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!'"
That pause before 'Halves!' — you can hear Wegg's entire moral architecture resting on that single syllable.
And then — 'it might be more according to the rights of things to say Two-thirds... Three-fourths.'
He is always open to correction, he says — gravely, generously, as though conducting a board meeting.
The prose style mimics Wegg's own inflated self-importance so perfectly — all those 'That' clauses, one after another.
It's free indirect discourse used for comic assassination — we're inside Wegg's grandiose logic, and the grandiosity itself is the joke.
And crucially, it ends with that glorious coda — he might be wrong about 'Halves,' he might deserve more.
Dickens gives Wegg the rope, and Wegg hangs himself with it, cheerfully.
One is reminded here of Burke's observation that vice loses half its evil by losing all its grossness.
Wegg is not merely greedy — he is greedy with ceremony, with rhetoric, with a kind of professional dignity.
He is an entire satirical portrait of the man who believes his appetites to be his rights.
What makes the comedy so corrosive is that such men do exist, and they flourish.
And of course Wegg's physical comedy is just as sharp as his verbal comedy.
Caroline, there's a moment with a keyhole that I know you love.
Oh, the grindstone scene is extraordinary — I think it's one of the funniest images in the whole novel.
Wegg says nothing — and that's the masterstroke — he simply mimes.
Listen to this:
"Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home."
'Laughed silently' — that's the detail that haunts you.
It's the laugh of someone utterly secure in their power, who doesn't need to be heard.
And then 'stumped home' — that gait, that wooden leg, that utterly undignified exit.
The imaginary grindstone is a beautiful piece of pantomime — and it's also precise information about their relationship.
Wegg is making Boffin grind — making him labour — through pure theatrical intimidation.
The comedy doesn't soften the power dynamic — it makes it starker, actually.
You laugh, and then you notice what you laughed at, and that's a slightly uncomfortable feeling.
There is also something in that scene about the limits of the comic mode itself.
Wegg's grotesquerie has kept us entertained, but Boffin stooping at the keyhole is a man humiliated.
Dickens knows when to let the comedy turn cold.
That, I think, is part of his genius — the tonal shift happens so fast you scarcely feel it until it has already occurred.
And of course Wegg's comedy has consequences — and eventually, justice.
Caroline, the scene where he finally meets his match is one I suspect you've savoured.
Wegg has been building to this for so long — the sneering, the 'That,' the grindstone — and then Harmon simply grabs him.
No rhetoric, no ceremony.
The novel gives us the moment with almost cinematic precision:
"He found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there."
Four actions, four semicolons, four stages of humiliation in perfect sequence.
Wegg was 'entering on some sarcastic retort' — and Dickens stops him mid-sentence with physical reality.
It's deeply, deeply satisfying.
The sentence structure does the comic work there — each semicolon is another shove.
Dickens is a great user of the list for physical violence — the accumulation of blows has a rhythm that prose can replicate almost bodily.
And 'his boundless amazement' — that phrase is pure comedy.
Wegg has genuinely not considered that anyone might simply seize him.
There is a moral satisfaction here that goes beyond comedy, I think.
Wegg has constructed an entire system of power based on documents and rhetoric — and it collapses before a man who simply acts.
Dickens understood something that Johnson understood: that moral pretension, however elaborate, is fragile.
The comedy here is the comedy of reality reasserting itself.
And before we leave the comic villains — there's one more figure who deserves a moment.
The Deputy Lock — who takes Betty Higden's coins one by one, then wipes his brow.
Dickens gives him perhaps the perfect sentence of hypocritical self-presentation:
"I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow" — and here he drew his sleeve across his forehead — "and I won't stand in your way."
He pockets her coins while declaring his virtue.
It's miniature — almost a cartoon — but it's absolutely exact.
That miniature portrait is so characteristic — the small hypocrite caught in one gesture.
The sleeve drawn across the forehead as though the coins were honestly earned — it's devastating in three words.
Our Mutual Friend is full of such moments — the comedy of surfaces, and the moral darkness just beneath.
We'll be back shortly to look at the novel's language in a very different register.

segments.title: Narrative Architecture: How Dickens Weaves Character and Plot

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — sentence by sentence, character by character.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the most audacious pieces of narrative engineering in all of Victorian fiction.
John Harmon is dead — except he isn't — and Dickens has constructed an elaborate architecture of disguise, self-examination, and moral testing around that central deception.
To help us unpack how it all holds together, I'm delighted to welcome three exceptional readers.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and thinks about the architecture of fiction the way a structural engineer thinks about a cathedral.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the moral imagination is at the heart of every great novel — and reads Dickens accordingly.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and brings a reader's passionate intimacy to every page.
Let's begin with John Harmon's great soliloquy — the moment he speaks himself back into existence and explains, to himself as much as to us, why he chose to disappear.
What strikes me first about these chapters is the almost unprecedented narrative risk Dickens takes.
He gives John Harmon a sustained interior monologue — pages of it — very late in the novel, when we've already been living with the mystery for hundreds of pages.
And the voice of that monologue is extraordinary — it's a man literally talking himself into clarity.
Listen to how Dickens renders the moment of his return to England.
"I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife."
That triple repetition — shrinking, shrinking, mistrustful — it's almost like someone shuddering.
Dickens is using syntax to enact the psychology — the sentence structure is the emotional state.
I think Eleanor is right about the formal daring, though I'd frame the achievement rather differently.
What Dickens is doing in that passage is something the great moralists have always done — he is showing us a conscience at work.
John Harmon is not merely explaining himself; he is subjecting himself to a rigorous moral audit.
Note that small, extraordinary moment at the end of the passage — he addresses himself directly.
"Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so."
That is a man holding himself accountable — no evasion, no special pleading.
Dr. Johnson would have recognised the form instantly — it is the examined life, conducted in prose.
What moves me is the loneliness of that self-address.
He has no one to confide in — no friend, no advocate — so he becomes his own interlocutor.
And that loneliness is rooted in something Dickens makes very specific — the childhood that produced it.
The key phrase for me comes slightly later, when Harmon recalls lying in that public-house bed.
"The dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil."
That word — perpetuating — carries so much weight.
He isn't just afraid for himself — he's afraid of becoming another link in a chain of harm.
And this is where the narrative architecture becomes genuinely intricate — because Dickens then shows us, in the next chapter, how that first simple intention spiralled beyond all control.
There's a remarkable sentence in chapter thirty-one that describes the mechanism of that drift.

"When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days."
That parenthetical — never yet for good within his knowledge then — is doing enormous work.
The word then is everything — it implies that good will eventually come, that this story does not end in the darkness it begins with.
Dickens embeds the shape of his whole plot into a single adverb.
That is a genuinely fine observation, and I shan't quarrel with it.
But I want to press on what happens when the deception does escape his control — because the moral predicament Dickens constructs is perfectly merciless.
Harmon realises he is trapped between two forms of dishonour — buying Bella or punishing her.
Dickens states it with a precision that is almost brutal.
"Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?"
Each horn of the dilemma carries its own precise moral charge — shame on one side, meanness on the other.
This is not social observation — this is a novelist thinking hard about what it means to act well under impossible conditions.
And all of this moral weight exists alongside moments that are purely, wonderfully comic — which is one of the things I love most about these chapters.
Mr Boffin's tirade against charity patronage titles is one of the funniest things in the book.
It arrives completely unexpectedly, and the rhythm of it is irresistible.

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
Up to his neck — that image is perfect, because of course Rokesmith really is drowning, just not in correspondence.
Dickens plants that comic moment right in the middle of chapters of tragic self-examination — and it doesn't break the spell; it deepens it.
That tonal range is Dickens's greatest technical gift, and these chapters demonstrate it brilliantly.
But the moment that I keep returning to is a small, almost wordless scene — Rokesmith watching from a doorway.
Dickens renders it in a single sentence, and it is one of the most quietly devastating in the whole novel.

"The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism."
Three characters, three trajectories, held in one sustained visual field — and Rokesmith can only look on.
The phrase 'boofer lady' — Betty Higden's childlike term of endearment — placed inside the Secretary's cold, detached point of view creates this extraordinary double register.
Away from paralysis and pauperism — I find that phrase extraordinary.
Betty Higden's whole story — her terror of the workhouse, her fierce self-reliance — is compressed into four words.
And yet the sentence is not a polemic — it is a picture.
Steady bright eyes trudging through the streets — that is character, not argument.
And Rokesmith watching her go — still watching even when she has disappeared into the streets — that is the image of a man who has forfeited the right to act.
He is a spectator in his own life — which is precisely what his deception has made him.
Dickens makes you feel that imprisonment without ever spelling it out.
Rokesmith standing in a doorway, watching the world he cannot yet enter — that image will stay with me.

We've seen tonight how Dickens uses interior monologue, syntactic rhythm, comic set-piece, and silent tableau — all within the same stretch of chapters — to build a portrait of a man caught between who he was and who he might become.
My thanks to Dr. Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt for bringing their very different and very complementary gifts to these pages.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the river — and what Dickens makes of the Thames as the great symbolic spine of this novel.
Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as a work of extraordinary ambition and strangeness.
Today we're examining what this novel does with money — the dust heaps, the wills, the charity rackets, and the social performances that wealth makes possible.
With me are three guests who have lived with this novel and thought hard about what it's doing.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for narrative architecture is, frankly, formidable.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes that moral imagination — not social programme — is the beating heart of great fiction.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read this novel more times than most people have read any novel, and who cares passionately about the experience on the page.
Let's begin with how Dickens introduces his social world — and the extraordinary figure of Twemlow.
Twemlow is, I think, one of the most quietly devastating comic inventions in the whole of English fiction.
Dickens introduces him not as a man but as a piece of furniture — and holds to that conceit with absolute precision.
Listen to the construction of the thing.
"Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state."
The word 'requisition' does extraordinary work there — it is a word for supplies, for materiel, not for human beings.
And then the dining-table metaphor is extended with what I can only call clinical thoroughness — leaves added, pulled out, positioned ever further from the centre.
The further from the centre of power, the further from the centre of the table — the metaphor and the social reality are perfectly, mercilessly aligned.
And what I love — from a craft perspective — is that Dickens never breaks the conceit to wink at us.
He commits to 'innocent piece of dinner-furniture' and then follows that logic wherever it leads, right through to 'the sideboard at one end of the room, or the window-curtains at the other.'
That is a structural choice — sustained metaphor as characterisation — and it tells us something devastatingly precise about Twemlow's social existence.
He is useful, he is peripheral, and the more he is used, the more peripheral he becomes.
Dickens has compressed an entire social tragedy into a joke about furniture.
What strikes me when I read it aloud — and I have, many times — is that Twemlow is never ridiculous.
The joke is entirely on the Veneerings and on the system that produces them.
He is 'innocent' — that's the first word Dickens uses about him.
He goes 'upon easy castors' — there's something almost tender in that image, this gentle man trundled about for other people's purposes.
And he is kept — when not in use — over a livery stable-yard.
He has no existence, Dickens implies, except when class and connection require him.
That tension between usefulness and dignity runs through everything in this novel.
And when Dickens turns his attention to the Boffins — to what sudden money actually attracts — the satire becomes something almost ferocious.
Caroline, you've been sitting with those passages about the letters that pour into the Boffin household — what do you make of them?
They are extraordinary passages.
Dickens catalogs the approaches of every conceivable kind of beggar — institutional and individual — with this manic, almost breathless energy.
And then he stops and reads us a letter — a real specimen, in full.
The setup is simply this:
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Six words of description, and you can see the thing perfectly — the weight of it, the pomposity, the absurdity.
And the letter itself is magnificent — all flattery and condescension, right down to the postscript limiting the steward's fee to three guineas.
The postscript is the masterstroke.
Dickens notes, with perfect deadpan, that the letter is 'Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of Linseed — and thoughtful in the postscript.'
The irony is so controlled it barely announces itself.
And then the revelation — the letter is 'lithographed by the hundred,' a form letter presenting 'but a pale individuality of an address.'
The Duke has not written to Boffin at all — a machine has.
It is a perfect image of how aristocratic condescension industrialises itself, applies scale to contempt.
And then Dickens pivots to the individual beggars, and the tone shifts almost imperceptibly — there's still satire, but there's something else.
He sets up the whole category of 'documents' with a line that is — I think — one of the funniest and saddest in the novel.
He writes that these beggars enclose 'documents' — and then says:
"they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
That simile is grotesque and precise and slightly horrible — and it tells you everything about how Dickens views the gap between the claim and the reality of these petitions.
But then comes the daughters of officers 'long accustomed to every luxury of life — except spelling.'
That parenthesis — 'except spelling' — is three words doing the work of a paragraph.
The 'inspired beggars' are what stay with me, though.
They were sitting over a fragment of candle — 'when surely some Angel whispered the name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls.'
There's a cruelty in that satire — these are real people, real desperation, and Dickens knows it.
The ones who will 'make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday' — the punctuality of their threatened suicide is terrible and funny at once.
Dickens holds both responses — laughter and discomfort — in the same sentence.
One resists, I think, the temptation to read this as a tract on poverty alone.
What Dickens is anatomising is something more uncomfortable — the corruption of the moral imagination by money.
These beggars are not simply poor — they are performing poverty, weaponising sentiment, confecting divine inspiration.
The golden dustman's arrival has degraded everyone who comes near the gold — not because the gold is tainted, but because human nature, unguarded, is corruptible.
That is the novel's great moral burden, and it is borne with remarkable evenhandedness.
And nobody illustrates that corruption of character by proximity to money more vividly than Bella Wilfer.
Eleanor, you wanted to talk about a moment where Bella's inner voice is — quite startlingly — exposed.
Yes — it's a brief passage but it's crystalline.
Bella is furious with Rokesmith — the secretary — for what she perceives as his presumption in paying her attention.
And she thinks, with magnificent indignation:
"A little too much, I think, to have Pa's lodger laying claim to me, and keeping eligible people off!"
'Eligible people' — that is doing all the work.
She doesn't want love — she wants access, she wants the right suitors, she wants her new position to yield its proper commercial return.
And Dickens renders her self-awareness as zero — she is entirely unironic about this, which is what makes her simultaneously infuriating and oddly endearing.
She's so honest in her dishonesty — that's the thing.
She says the quiet part absolutely at full volume, inside her own head.
The 'opportunities opened to me by Mr and Mrs Boffin' — she sees her position there as a set of opportunities to be appropriated, not as generosity to be grateful for.
Rokesmith is merely a 'mere Secretary and Pa's lodger' — and the contempt in those words is perfectly calibrated.
We are meant to find her awful here, and we do — and yet there's something so recognisably human in the grievance.
She is a character in the process of being tested — and failing, at this stage, rather badly.
The novel is, among other things, a story about whether Bella can recover her better nature from the corrupting influence of money and expectation.
Which brings us, inevitably, to what money actually means in this world — the will, the dust heaps, the original Harmon bequest.
Wegg — the wooden-legged man who has insinuated himself into the Boffin household and believes he has found a will that will undo everything — reads out what he imagines to be a devastating document.
He announces, with great satisfaction:

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
The bleakness of that document — 'never made friends,' 'rebellious family' — is extraordinary.
Old Harmon's will is a biography compressed into a legal instrument — and it is a biography entirely without love.
And 'quite enough for him' — three words about Boffin that contain everything old Harmon thought of him.
Not generous, not affectionate — just sufficient.
Structurally, it's fascinating that Dickens presents the will through Wegg — the great schemer, the manipulator — reading it aloud for his own purposes.
The document that might contain the truth about the Boffin fortune is mediated through the least trustworthy voice in the room.
That is a craft decision — and it's brilliant, because it means we can never quite settle on what the truth of the money is.
That uncertainty — about what money really means, who really owns it, what it actually confers — seems to be the novel's central anxiety.
The dust heaps are both literal and symbolic from the very first pages — wealth made of refuse, inheritance built on what other people threw away.
We'll return to what the novel does with all of this as we move deeper into the story — but for now, my thanks to Eleanor, Edmund, and Caroline for an exceptional conversation.
We've come a long way through this novel tonight — through the river and the dust heaps, through disguises and discoveries.
And I want to close by asking what the novel finally offers us — if anything — by way of redemption.
Because this is a book full of wreckage — moral, social, physical — and yet it never quite loses its faith in human goodness.
Eleanor, I want to start with you — because I think you've been circling something all evening about how Dickens holds these contradictions together.
Yes — and I think the key to it all is that Dickens refuses to let virtue be fashionable.
There's a moment with the Boffins that I find absolutely disarming in its simplicity.
Mr Boffin turns to his wife — this warm, ungainly, genuinely good woman — and says:
"Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!"
And Dickens's narrator immediately tells us this was ruin to Mrs Boffin's social aspirations — and that they sat together, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.
That capital U on Unfashionable — Dickens earns that little joke.
The satire and the tenderness arrive in the same breath, and somehow the tenderness wins.
That passage exemplifies precisely what I value most in this novel.
The Boffins are not redeemed by circumstances improving around them — they simply are good, and that goodness endures against every fashionable pressure.
But I confess the character that haunts me as this novel closes is Bradley Headstone.
Because Dickens gives him something far more terrible than remorse.
The narrator is quite precise about this — let me read it carefully:
"He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently."
That is a genuinely profound psychological insight — and it is rendered not in the language of theology, but in the language of compulsion.
Headstone is not punished from without; he is destroyed by the machinery of his own unrepentant nature.
Edmund's reading of Headstone moves me — and frightens me a little, if I'm honest.
That passage about doing the deed a thousand times — it reads almost like a definition of hell.
And Dickens has prepared us for exactly this kind of darkness much earlier in the novel, through the most extraordinary landscape writing.
There is a moment when Eugene is on the river, being followed, and the sun goes down —
"And then the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that blood, guiltily shed, does."
Every time I read that sentence I have to stop.
The landscape itself is already mourning — before the violence has even happened.
That is what makes the horror of Headstone so complete — the world around him has been stained in advance.
Caroline's point about the landscape anticipating the crime is exactly right — and it connects to something structural.
Dickens uses the natural world not as decoration but as moral register throughout this novel.
And Riderhood's accusation of Gaffer Hexam gives us the same quality — the language of sworn testimony made to feel almost incantatory.
Listen to the rhythm when Riderhood makes his declaration:
"The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
That repetition of 'hand' — three times in two sentences — turns accusation into something almost liturgical.
And it's coming from Riderhood — one of the least reliable, most self-serving characters in the book.
Dickens keeps the moral ground shifting under us, even in the novel's darkest passages.
Eleanor is right to flag Riderhood — and I think his presence illuminates something about this novel's moral vision.
Dickens does not give us redeemable villains and irredeemable ones in neat piles.
Headstone is educated, respectable, consumed by passion — and he condemns himself by the architecture of his own mind.
Whilst the Boffins — blundering, good-hearted, and quite hopelessly Unfashionable — simply endure and remain themselves.
That, I would suggest, is a deeply conservative moral: character is destiny, and goodness needs no programme.
I'm not sure I'd call it conservative so much as — irreducible.
Dickens seems to believe that goodness can exist in the worst circumstances, but he never pretends the circumstances don't hurt.
What stays with me from tonight — and from the novel — is that image of Mr and Mrs Boffin sitting side by side.
Unfashionable, yes. Ruin to her aspirations, yes.
But there — present — together. And Dickens clearly thinks that counts for something enormous.
I think that may be the most fitting note on which to close.
A novel full of murder, obsession, and social cruelty — and yet its deepest image is two people sitting quietly together, and being glad of each other.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers who have made this extraordinary novel feel new again tonight.
Our Mutual Friend Unpacked will return. Until then — keep reading.

      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God

      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),

      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

‘Now, scoundrel,’ said John Harmon, taking another sailor-like turn on his
      cravat and holding him in his corner at arms’ length, ‘I shall make two
      more short speeches to you, because I hope they will torment you. Your
      discovery was a genuine discovery (such as it was), for nobody had thought
      of looking into that place. Neither did we know you had made it, until
      Venus spoke to Mr Boffin, though I kept you under good observation from my
      first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief
      occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow. I tell
      you this, that you may know we knew enough of you to persuade Mr Boffin to
      let us lead you on, deluded, to the last possible moment, in order that
      your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment. That’s
      the first short speech, do you understand?’

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.

c30:p22.text:
‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity
      that dates from my childhood with my poor sister.

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,

      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do

c2:p2.text:
There was an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy
      castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint
      James’s, when not in use, to whom the Veneerings were a source of blind
      confusion. The name of this article was Twemlow. Being first cousin to
      Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might
      be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state. Mr and Mrs
      Veneering, for example, arranging a dinner, habitually started with
      Twemlow, and then put leaves in him, or added guests to him. Sometimes,
      the table consisted of Twemlow and half a dozen leaves; sometimes, of
      Twemlow and a dozen leaves; sometimes, Twemlow was pulled out to his
      utmost extent of twenty leaves. Mr and Mrs Veneering on occasions of
      ceremony faced each other in the centre of the board, and thus the
      parallel still held; for, it always happened that the more Twemlow was
      pulled out, the further he found himself from the center, and nearer to
      the sideboard at one end of the room, or the window-curtains at the other.
c2:p2.summary: Twemlow, a man of good family connections, is introduced through an extended metaphor comparing him to a dining table that the Veneerings manipulate for social purposes.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly
      witnessed, very short. Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever
      had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the
      Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and

      they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.
c9:p28.summary: Mr Boffin lovingly affirms his wife's moral character, but Dickens narrates that their virtuous intentions doom their social aspirations to fashionability.
c9:p28.best_quote: Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!

c57:p53.text:
Now, too, was he cursed with a state of mind more wearing and more
      wearisome than remorse. He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold
      that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing
      the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently. In the defensive
      declarations and pretended confessions of murderers, the pursuing shadow
      of this torture may be traced through every lie they tell. If I had done
      it as alleged, is it conceivable that I would have made this and this
      mistake? If I had done it as alleged, should I have left that unguarded
      place which that false and wicked witness against me so infamously deposed
      to? The state of that wretch who continually finds the weak spots in his
      own crime, and strives to strengthen them when it is unchangeable, is a
      state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times
      instead of once; but it is a state, too, that tauntingly visits the
      offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment
      every time.
c57:p53.summary: The narrator explores the psychological torment of murderers without remorse: they are compelled to endlessly re-enact and mentally perfect their crime, creating a torture worse than remorse itself.
c57:p53.best_quote: He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently.

c51:p62.text:
The boat went on, under the arching trees, and over their tranquil shadows
      in the water. The bargeman skulking on the opposite bank of the stream,
      went on after it. Sparkles of light showed Riderhood when and where the
      rower dipped his blades, until, even as he stood idly watching, the sun
      went down and the landscape was dyed red. And then the red had the
      appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that
      blood, guiltily shed, does.
c51:p62.summary: As Bradley pursues Eugene into the fading light, the reddening landscape evokes blood guiltily shed, mounting to heaven—a foreshadowing of tragic violence.
c51:p62.best_quote: And then the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that blood, guiltily shed, does.

c12:p93.text:
‘Now let me be took down again,’ said Riderhood, when he had turned the
      drowned cap over and under, and had brushed it the wrong way (if it had a
      right way) with his sleeve. ‘I give information that the man that done the
      Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body. The hand of
      Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the
      hand that done that deed. His hand and no other.’
c12:p93.summary: Riderhood solemnly accuses Gaffer Hexam of committing the Harmon murder, declaring with certainty that it was Gaffer's hand that committed the deed.
